Property & Land Law Practice Guide

Inheritance, Succession, and Bakaspatra (Gift Deeds) in Nepalese Land Law

📅 Published: 2025-05-05
🔄 Updated: 2025-10-01
⏱ 8 min read
🔍 Review: Senior Advocate Lead Counsel, Supreme Court Bar Association
Direct Legal Answer & Overview

In Nepal, transfer of property without monetary consideration occurs through Bakaspatra (Gift Deeds / बकसपत्र) or statutory succession upon death (Apunstrali). Under the Muluki Civil Code 2074, a person can freely gift their self-acquired property, but cannot execute a Bakaspatra of ancestral property without the written consent of all adult co-heirs (Anshiyars). A registered Bakaspatra executed in violation of co-heir partition rights can be challenged and nullified in court through a Deed Cancellation Lawsuit (Likhit Badr Mudda) within statutory limitation.

Key Practical Takeaways

  • Ancestral property cannot be gifted via Bakaspatra without co-heir consent.
  • Conditional gift deeds (Haldekhibako Bakaspatra) transfer immediate ownership.
  • Deed cancellation suits must be filed within statutory limitation (typically 2 years from knowledge).

Transferring family real estate through Bakaspatra (बकसपत्र / Gift Deed) is a deeply ingrained practice in Nepal. While gift deeds allow owners to transfer property voluntarily to relatives without commercial sale consideration, improper execution frequently triggers acrimonious inheritance lawsuits under the Muluki Civil Code 2074.

1. Legal Restrictions on Gifting Ancestral Property

The most common ground for litigation arises when an aging father or mother executes a Bakaspatra transferring prime ancestral property to one preferred child, bypassing other sons and daughters. Under Chapter 14 of the Civil Code, an owner possesses absolute freedom to gift self-acquired property. However, gifting ancestral property without the written consent of all adult co-heirs is unlawful, and aggrieved heirs can file a lawsuit for cancellation of the deed (Likhit Badr).

2. Intestate Succession Hierarchy (Apunstrali)

When a property owner passes away without leaving a registered will (Ichhapatra) or gift deed, their estate passes under the statutory succession rules of Apunstrali (अपुताली). The estate descends in strict statutory order: first to surviving spouse and children equally; if none, to parents; if none, to brothers and sisters; and subsequently to more distant collaterals (Hakwala).

Statutory Citations & Governing Nepal Legislation

Statute / Act Section / Rule Legal Significance
Muluki Civil Code 2074 Chapter 14 (Provisions Relating to Gift/Donation) Rules governing execution and validity of Bakaspatra deeds.
Muluki Civil Code 2074 Chapter 16 (Provisions Relating to Succession) Statutory succession hierarchy when an owner dies without a will.

Documentary Checklist for this Procedure

  • ✔ Original registered Bakaspatra deed copy from Malpot Office
  • ✔ Ward Relationship Certificate proving coparcenary status
  • ✔ Lalpurja of disputed land plot

Frequently Asked Questions on this Topic

Can a person revoke a Bakaspatra after it has been registered at the Malpot Office?

Under Section 226 of the Civil Code, an unconditional registered gift deed (Haldekhibako Bakaspatra) cannot be unilaterally revoked once executed and delivered, unless the deed explicitly included statutory conditions that the recipient failed to fulfill.
